description.p: Lambdock is a desktop dock for GNU/Linux, in the spirit of Cairo-Dock, Plank and the reference dock. It is built with GTK4 and, on Wayland, gtk4-layer-shell; on X11 it docks itself through EWMH. It can be themed, extended and reconfigured live with GNU Guile Scheme.
Features include:

ul.li: Dynamic window tracking: the Wayland foreign-toplevel protocol, or EWMH on X11
Multi-monitor support and multiple dock instances
GTK CSS themes and configurable application launchers
Dynamic widgets for CPU, RAM, temperature and more
An embedded Guile runtime with hot-reloading and an optional REPL

screenshot.caption: Lambdock as a floating dock, with a folder stack open
The launchpad, filtered by its search field
Preferences: every dock setting, applied live
Taskbar mode with the Luna theme and dynamic widgets

description.p: An X11 session gets a dock now, not an ordinary window in the corner. The dock speaks EWMH on a connection of its own: the window list, titles, application ids and window state come from the standard root and per-window properties, and focus, close and minimize are the standard requests. Its own window declares itself a dock, sits on the configured edge and publishes a strut, so maximized windows stop at the dock instead of covering it. Auto-hide needs a surface a compositor can push off screen, so it stays off on X11 and the dock says so once. GNOME on Wayland implements neither protocol; it now names what is missing. X11 support is optional at build time: a GTK built without the X11 backend still builds a Wayland-only dock.

The unit tests no longer resolve icons through the icon theme of the desktop running them. They used whatever theme was configured, so on a desktop whose theme lacks utilities-terminal the dock logged its icon fallback and GLib's fatal-warning policy aborted the accessibility and dock-item suites. The build now pins the test icon theme to Adwaita through a fixture XDG_CONFIG_HOME; no assertion changed, and the suite is green on a machine that ships neither Adwaita's application icons nor utilities-terminal.

The showcase recording plays 1.25x faster, shows each theme family on a wallpaper of its own temperature (galaxy, mountain haze, warm dusk, blue ocean) and closes by applying the settings this machine runs to the live dock: Platinum on its shelf at -17 with 48 px icons five pixels apart. The popover row that the previous rename had mangled reads "Close All" again, and the guide is rewritten in the register of the thing it describes.

The manual is split into eight pages under docs/, one per task (getting started, the dock itself, configuration, theming and the shelf, the REPL, internals, development, contributing), and the README is a landing page that indexes them. Every heading kept its CUSTOM_ID and every cross-reference was rewritten to the page that now owns the section, with all file and anchor links resolved against the tree. No code changed.

Startup and a hot reload now read the dock's settings through one reader instead of each reading its own subset. A reload used to build its stylesheet before it had read the new icon size, so the shelf indicator was decided from the previous size; the same split is how a setting could reach one path and not the other.

Every theme and look is now named after its material, not after the desktop it was traced from: Brushed, Frost, Platinum, Dune, Stage and Glass join Luna, Aurora, Seven, Tiles and Island, and the old names and short aliases are removed. A settings file that still names an old theme resolves to the default, and the changelog carries the migration table.

Popover menus keep the dock's own material again: the shelf modifier no longer repaints them, and every hovered row clears WCAG AA contrast against its background. The worst case across the nineteen themes is 4.50:1.
The shelf is also laid out on the first frame now, instead of waiting for the next reload, and the dock's runtime state paths are named in one place.

Every running application painted its indicator twice: the theme draws a dot at the bottom of the button, and the glass shelf draws its own bead on the slab. The rule that was supposed to silence the theme's dot sat in the shelf stylesheet, which is loaded before the theme -- and GTK resolves competing declarations from providers of the same priority by the order they were added, not by specificity, so the rule never won.

The suppression is now attached after the theme, only while the glass actually draws the bead, and the user's own stylesheet still wins over both. A test renders a button in both states and asserts the pixels.

Separators, gauges and clocks keep their reserved reflection band -- they line up with the icons beside them -- but they no longer cast the icon's contact shadow, which is the pool an icon makes on the glass and had no business hanging under a divider.

The running indicator reads again: the bead is larger than the reference's 12x3px proportions, drawn as a bar with crisp edges rather than a blob that fades in every direction, and the dark pool under it is tight enough to sit around the bead instead of turning the whole band into a grey smear.

Changes made in the Preferences window, by dragging icons around, or by anything else writing the local state under ~/.local/state/lambdock are now picked up as they happen: the dock watches that directory and re-reads its settings when it settles, and a preference is persisted before it is applied.

The Platinum material is no longer an estimate. The install image carries the real the reference dock, so the platinum slab is measured off its own artwork: the outer lip is 1px of black with 2px of white in front of it that brightens towards the middle of the dock, the drop shadow starts at 0.60 against the slab and fades over 18px, the running indicator is a 12x3 white bead on a 54x12 cyan glow, the folder panel is charcoal with a light bevel, and the divider is a two-pixel engraved groove.

The side-dock indicator got its own measurements (it is a tall bead on a narrow glow, not the bottom one rotated), and the contact shadow under each icon is the elliptical pool the real dock had instead of a grey stripe -- which is what had kept that decoration switched off. The dock's menus also follow the reference dock's wording: "Open" for an application, a stack and the trash, and "View content as a grid/list" for a stack's view switch.

Dragging an icon out of the dock now bursts it into a puff of smoke, as the real dock did: a third of a second of smoke sized to the icon, in the icon's own place, with the dock keeping its width until the puff clears and the remaining icons closing the gap afterwards. The burst is deterministic arithmetic in the core (fourteen puffs that start spread out, travel outwards and die from the outside in) drawn by a frame-clock widget, so both halves are tested -- the cloud without a display, the widget in a real window.
The round that finished the list of known rough edges. Nothing about how the dock behaves changed; what changed is where the code keeps its values and who owns them.

The meter's geometry and its green/amber/red thresholds are now pure, unit-tested functions, and the drawing code only paints what they describe. The glass shelf's value types moved into the pure core layer, so the core headers no longer include the application header or a widget header -- and the application header no longer includes libguile.h at all, because the only Scheme value it carried is an opaque handle now.

Dynamic-item pollers go through the Guile bridge (one opaque handle in, one plain reading out), the desktop-entry cache is a single value with one owner, the icon search paths are built from explicit inputs and tested, and the dock's window model (tracking, running/focused/minimized styling and the app-id lookup) moved out of dock_item.c into its own file.

Two theme families, and whole-dock recipes. Brushed (the flat gloss strip the icons sit inside) and Glass (the 26 Liquid Glass pill, light and dark) join the built-in themes, Frost's dock now carries its own 3D shelf material, and Aurora and Seven (the glass superbar) complete the taskbar family, which is now consistent: all five are taskbars, all draw 32px icons, and they differ only where their era did.

Twenty look recipes set a whole dock in one line -- "(define dock-look 'platinum-dark)" brings the theme, the icon size and spacing, the end padding, the dock/taskbar mode, the window titles and every glass-shelf number, plus the fisheye, because shelf docks magnify and no taskbar did. Anything you define yourself still wins, and "(apply-look! 'glass)" restyles a running dock. Every recipe is unit tested for completeness.

Polish across all nineteen themes: the focused window now has its own indicator everywhere (the long taskbar underline, the wide Island pill, a brighter glow on the stock themes), every theme colours its window titles, the light shelf docks get dark labels and dark running dots so nothing vanishes into pale glass, and theme scoping no longer loses a selector written across two lines -- which is what used to let one theme's indicator paint under another's icons.

The launchpad loses its "Applications" title -- the grid of what is installed is the screen -- and its close button sits on the left by default, with a new dock-launchpad-close-side setting (and Preferences row) to move it to the right. The Preferences window gains a "Dock items" card that appends a trash can, a clock, or a RAM, CPU, temperature or battery meter to the dock, stored with the drag-and-drop layout so it survives a restart.

Measured where a hover frame's time goes: the dock's own magnification arithmetic costs about 30 microseconds per frame (0.2% of a frame), while the process reads zero CPU when idle or hidden and about 7% of one core during an active hover sweep -- so the remaining cost is GTK laying the row out and painting it, which is what magnification is.

Edge behaviour audited with a real pointer: nothing is clipped at the ends of the row, the row widens without jumping vertically, and the screen edge does not bounce (12 rapid crossings in and out of the dock give zero hides; 12 jitters along the reveal strip give exactly one reveal).

Auto-hide reveals again. The input region that makes the trigger strip reachable was set but never committed -- Wayland surface state is double buffered and a dock that has finished sliding draws nothing -- so the compositor kept the dock-shaped region and the strip stayed dead. It now asks for the frame that commits it.

A pointer that rests on the strip while the dock slides away under it never crosses back into it, so motion on the strip now reveals the dock, not only a crossing. A reveal that arrives while a hide is starting is turned around instead of dropped, and a leave is only ignored while the dock is actually moving. The strip itself is 4 px instead of 2, and LAMBDOCK_DEBUG=1 traces the whole sequence with timestamps.

Packaging fix: the render-budget test skips itself when there is no display server instead of aborting inside gtk_init, so a sandboxed package build's check phase passes. Nothing changed in the dock itself.

Auto-hide works again: while the dock is tucked away or sliding, the whole surface takes input, because the only part of it on screen is the trigger strip -- which the dock-shaped input region had cut away. Once the dock is out, the region is the slab plus the icons again, and it is only re-set when it changes.

The hover path is now measured and tested rather than eyeballed: render counters record layout steps, geometry-cache rebuilds, paints and surface resizes, and a test drives the real hover path to assert the budget (no surface resizes, fewer geometry rebuilds than frames, and no work at all for sub-pixel pointer jitter). Item geometry is cached per layout change instead of re-queried every frame.

Hovering the dock no longer resizes it. Growing the icons under the pointer made GTK resize the window, and on Wayland that means a buffer re-allocation and a compositor reconfigure on every pointer frame -- the flicker and torn pixels along the dock's edges. The room the row spreads into is reserved once, before the pointer starts magnifying, so the surface keeps its size for the whole hover.

The reserved room (including the headroom the dock always had above its capsule) is now cut out of the surface's input region, so the invisible band around the dock can no longer swallow clicks meant for the windows underneath.

The clock item is an analogue face instead of a time string: a squircle body with a brushed bezel, a paper dial, tick marks, three hands and a sweep of glass, all drawn from geometry so it stays crisp at any dock-icon-size. It keeps its own colours -- a watch face is an object -- and takes one icon cell instead of a string's width, and its hands follow the system clock while the item's poller keeps naming the reading for the tooltip and the screen reader.
The face's geometry is a pure function with its own test, and the showcase recording and stills are re-recorded with it.

Dynamic items line up with the icons beside them. A gauge, a separator and the clock used to measure shorter than an icon and hang at the bottom of the row; on a shelf theme the gauges also sat a whole reflection band lower, because a meter dropped the reflection slot that reserves that band. Every item now carries one icon-sized cell, keeps its reflection slot whether or not it has artwork to mirror, and a separator fills its cell.
The showcase recording and its stills are re-recorded with the fix.

The showcase recording now shows the two Platinum materials the way their stylesheet intends: the polished platinum slab with the icons mirrored onto the glass in front of them, which needs the dock's shelf geometry as well as the theme. The montage gives each of them a longer beat, and the REPL helper it teaches applies the theme and the geometry in one expression.

The Preferences scene shows the dialog on its own: the demo clears its terminals first, the popover row it clicks targets Close All again, and the dialog opens floating at the size the scene uses, clear of the caption. The taskbar scene is captioned for what it shows instead of promising window titles, which this layout measures away.

The showcase recording is now framed and captioned like a product video, and every scene in it was re-filmed and checked against its caption: auto-hide at the screen edge, fish-eye magnification, launching with running indicators, the window popover, the dock's own menu and the Preferences window, a folder stack, the launchpad filtered from the REPL, a live Guile REPL session changing the icon size and the themes, and the Luna taskbar mode. The recording now contains exactly one cursor -- the compositor's own -- instead of one drawn in post.

Also in this release: the launchpad search field takes the keyboard as soon as the launchpad opens, launching minimizes and restores the focused window on compositors that support it, larger launchpad tiles, a rebuilt Luna theme, and a quality pass over running the dock across compositors without wlr-layer-shell or wlr-foreign-toplevel.

Lambdock is now licensed under the MIT License, and every source file says so. Stacks no longer offer the fan view: the icon grid and the list remain, and a settings file that still asks for the fan reads back as the grid. Under the hood the C side was rebuilt around explicit models -- the launchpad, the preferences window and the set of active docks -- with their arithmetic and filtering moved into pure functions that are tested without a display.

The launchpad shows one tile per application again: desktop files that describe the same program, such as the distro package and the Flatpak export of it, are collapsed. A tile whose application is installed more than once offers which copy to start from its context menu, with where each copy comes from and the command it runs. The backdrop is denser, so the labels read over a busy desktop.
The right-click menu of a dock item now carries actions that fit the application: browsers get New Window and New Private Window, and a running music player gets playback controls over MPRIS.
The container image builds again: the Dockerfile now ships the desktop entry and AppStream metadata the build needs.
Keyboard and screen-reader accessibility with a reduce-motion setting, a rebuilt stack fan that shows live file thumbnails, a configurable launchpad, and a roomier preferences window.
Expanded test coverage and packaging improvements.
Improved RPM packaging and stability fixes.
Packaging and build refinements.
Added Podman/Docker builds and improved APT and RPM packaging.
